sentences.text: Massospondylus is a mid-sized sauropodomorph dinosaur whose name translates to 'longer vertebra'.

The animal possessed a small skull measuring about half the length of its femur and a vertebral column composed of nine neck vertebrae, thirteen back vertebrae, three hip vertebrae, and at least forty tail vertebrae.
Fossils of this dinosaur include clutches of eggs with embryos, representing some of the oldest amniote eggs and embryos known in the fossil record.
Excavations between 2005 and 2012 revealed ten egg clutches containing up to 34 eggs each at the Rooidraai nesting site.
Due to its abundance, Massospondylus defines the Massospondylus Range Zone, which serves as the uppermost biozone in the Karoo Supergroup.
The genus Massospondylus was named by Richard Owen in 1854 from South African remains, making it one of the first dinosaurs to be described by science.
As of 2019, the 'Big Momma' specimen is the largest and most complete Massospondylus found in Africa, though this fossil is divided into seven blocks with the heaviest weighing approximately 35 kg.

Massospondylus is now considered to have been bipedal, despite earlier depictions as quadrupedal, although a 2007 study by Bonnan and Senter argued that the animal was restricted to bipedal gaits rather than being quadrupedal.

The animal likely had a herbivorous or omnivorous diet, as cranial features resemble those of herbivorous reptiles more than carnivorous ones, yet it is debated whether basal sauropodomorphs like Massospondylus may have been omnivorous.

Gastroliths, or stomach stones, have been found associated with Massospondylus fossils in South Africa, confirming the animal swallowed stones to aid digestion, although a 2007 study by Wings and Sander argued these were likely not used as an effective gastric mill.
Analysis of the femur showed that Massospondylus growth was cyclic, forming one growth ring per year.
The ossification of the thumb in Massospondylus embryos before other limbs suggests it had important functions at early developmental stages.
Reisz and colleagues in 2005 suggested embryos were near hatching based on their size relative to the egg and advanced bone development.

Fossil tracks show both hindfoot and hand prints with outward-rotated hands, suggesting quadrupedal movement in juveniles, but a 2025 study noted the hatchling's humerus is incompletely preserved, making reliable posture estimation based on shaft circumference difficult.
Massospondylus is often classified within the family Massospondylidae.
In 1888, Lydekker classified Massospondylus as a dinosaur within the family Anchisauridae and the group Theropoda.
Massospondylus lived during the Hettangian, Sinemurian, and Pliensbachian ages, inhabiting Africa between 200 and 183 million years ago from the Hettangian to the Pliensbachian stages.
Most remains are found in the upper Elliot and Clarens Formations of South Africa and Lesotho, part of the Stormberg Group in the Karoo Supergroup.

Scientific understanding of this animal involves ongoing debates regarding its diet, with some arguing for omnivory, and its locomotion, with studies suggesting strict bipedalism despite track evidence of quadrupedalism in juveniles.
